hints: Follow the whole journey of water, from soil into the root and then all the way up the stem to the highest leaf. Where could each of the three listed processes act along that route?

Remember water always moves from higher to lower water potential. Think how osmosis loads water at the bottom, and how evaporation from leaves plus movement in narrow xylem vessels keeps pulling it upward.
walkthrough:
**Picture the gradient needed**

Think like the plant. Water must move continuously from soil (high water potential) to roots to stem to leaves to air (very low water potential).

To keep that flow going to the very top, the plant needs help at the bottom, in the middle, and at the top.

**Check each process in place**

Osmosis (2) moves water into root hairs and across root cells because root cell sap has a lower (more negative) water potential than soil water.

Capillarity (1) helps water rise a short way in the very narrow xylem vessels by adhesion to walls and cohesion between water molecules.

Transpiration (3) evaporates water from mesophyll cell walls, lowering their water potential and creating the strong transpiration pull that draws the whole column up.

**Put it together**

All three act at different points but all maintain the same downhill gradient from soil to air.

That is why 1, 2 and 3 are all responsible, which points to option A.

options.A: Correct. Osmosis drives uptake at roots, capillarity aids movement in narrow xylem, and transpiration creates the main pull from the top, so all three maintain the gradient.
options.B: Incomplete. It correctly includes capillarity and osmosis but wrongly leaves out transpiration, which provides the major pulling force.
options.C: Incomplete. It correctly includes capillarity and transpiration but wrongly leaves out osmosis, which is essential for water entry at the roots.
options.D: Incomplete. It correctly includes osmosis and transpiration but wrongly leaves out capillarity in the xylem vessels.
